questions.prompt: What does it mean for a square matrix \(A\) to have inverse \(A^{-1}\)?
questions.answer: It means multiplication by \(A^{-1}\) reverses multiplication by \(A\). The defining equations are \[AA^{-1}=I\quad\text{and}\quad A^{-1}A=I,\] where \(I\) is the identity matrix of the same size.

questions.prompt: Can a non-square matrix have an inverse in this course's matrix sense?
questions.answer: No. Inverses apply to square matrices only, because the identity matrix must have compatible size on both sides of the multiplication \(AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I\).

questions.prompt: Decide whether \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{pmatrix}\) is invertible.
questions.answer: Compute the determinant: \[2\cdot3-1\cdot5=6-5=1.\] Since the determinant is nonzero, the matrix is invertible.

questions.prompt: Decide whether \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&6\end{pmatrix}\) is singular.
questions.answer: Compute the determinant: \[1\cdot6-2\cdot3=6-6=0.\] Since the determinant is zero, the matrix is singular and has no inverse.

questions.prompt: Find the inverse of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: The determinant is \(3\cdot1-1\cdot2=1\). Therefore \[A^{-1}=\frac1{1}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Use an inverse to solve \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\end{pmatrix}\), given \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Multiply by \(A^{-1}\): \[\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5-6\\3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Check that \(B=\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\-5&2\end{pmatrix}\) is the inverse of \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Compute \[AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3&-1\\-5&2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6-5&-2+2\\15-15&-5+6\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Since the product gives \(I\), and these are square matrices, this verifies the inverse relationship.

questions.prompt: Find \(A^{-1}\) for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}4&7\\2&5\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: The determinant is \(4\cdot5-7\cdot2=20-14=6\). Therefore \[A^{-1}=\frac1{6}\begin{pmatrix}5&-7\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Solve \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}\) using an inverse.
questions.answer: The determinant is \(2\cdot1-1\cdot1=1\), so \[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \[\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: A student writes \(\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\1&3\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&\frac14\\1&\frac13\end{pmatrix}\). Explain the error and find the correct inverse.
questions.answer: Matrix inversion is not entry-wise reciprocation. The determinant is \(2\cdot3-4\cdot1=2\). The correct inverse is \[\frac1{2}\begin{pmatrix}3&-4\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac32&-2\\-\frac12&1\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: Explain why \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) has solution \(\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf b\) when \(A\) is invertible.
questions.answer: Start with \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\). Multiply both sides on the left by \(A^{-1}\): \[A^{-1}A\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf b.\] Since \(A^{-1}A=I\), this becomes \[I\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf b.\] Therefore \(\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf b\).

questions.prompt: For \(A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t&2\\8&t\end{pmatrix}\), classify the values of \(t\) for which \(A\) is invertible.
questions.answer: The determinant is \[t^2-16=(t-4)(t+4).\] The matrix is invertible exactly when the determinant is nonzero. Therefore \(A\) is invertible for \(t\ne4\) and \(t\ne-4\), and singular for \(t=\pm4\).

questions.prompt: Find \(a\) so that \(\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\a&9\end{pmatrix}\) has no inverse.
questions.answer: The matrix has no inverse when its determinant is zero. Compute \[\det=1\cdot9-a^2=9-a^2.\] Set this equal to zero: \[9-a^2=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad a^2=9.\] Thus \(a=3\) or \(a=-3\).

questions.prompt: A square matrix has inverse. Explain why its columns cannot be proportional in the \(2\times2\) case.
questions.answer: For a \(2\times2\) matrix, proportional columns make the determinant zero. If the columns are \(\begin{pmatrix}a\\c\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\lambda\begin{pmatrix}a\\c\end{pmatrix}\), the determinant is \(a\lambda c-\\lambda ac=0\). But an inverse exists exactly when the determinant is nonzero. Therefore an invertible \(2\times2\) matrix cannot have proportional columns.

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&5\end{pmatrix}\), compute \(A^{-1}\) and verify one multiplication order.
questions.answer: The determinant is \(1\cdot5-2\cdot3=-1\). Hence \[A^{-1}=\frac1{-1}\begin{pmatrix}5&-2\\-3&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-5&2\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] Verify: \[AA^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&5\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-5&2\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\]

questions.prompt: A student says that if \(AB=I\), then it is unnecessary to care about \(BA\). Discuss this for square matrices in this course.
questions.answer: The definition of inverse requires both \(AB=I\) and \(BA=I\). For square matrices of the same size, one identity product usually implies the other in standard linear algebra, but the definition is still two-sided because matrix multiplication is not generally commutative. Writing both equations prevents the common mistake of treating matrices like ordinary numbers.

questions.prompt: Explain why a singular matrix cannot be used to solve every equation \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf b\) by multiplying by \(A^{-1}\).
questions.answer: A singular matrix has \(\det(A)=0\), so \(A^{-1}\) does not exist. The step \(\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf b\) is therefore meaningless. Depending on \(\mathbf b\), the system may have no solution or infinitely many solutions, but there is no inverse matrix that gives a unique solution for every right-hand side.

questions.prompt: Prove that if \(A\) is invertible, then \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf0\) has only the trivial solution.
questions.answer: Start with \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf0\). Since \(A\) is invertible, multiply both sides on the left by \(A^{-1}\): \[A^{-1}A\mathbf{x}=A^{-1}\mathbf0.\] The left side is \(I\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}\), and the right side is \(\mathbf0\). Hence \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf0\), so the homogeneous system has only the trivial solution.
